summary: Deprecates MD5-based authentication for the Network Time Protocol, because MD5 is considered too weak, and recommends AES-CMAC (RFC 4493) as a replacement for the message authentication code. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC says NTP should stop using MD5 to authenticate packets because that method is too weak. It recommends AES-CMAC with a shared key for packets that use NTP authentication.

questions: why is md5 deprecated for ntp
subtitle: Deprecates MD5-based NTP authentication and recommends AES-CMAC instead.

tldr.problem: The NTP authentication method described in RFC 5905 uses MD5, which this memo says is not a secure message authentication code.
tldr.mechanism: When NTP authentication is used, implementations must compute AES-CMAC over the NTP header and any extension fields using a shared 128-bit AES key.
tldr.outcome: The memo deprecates MD5 authentication and recommends AES-CMAC. Unit metadata lists RFC 9748 as an update.

today: RFC 8573 is listed as a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9748, according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why NTP Authentication Changes
sections.content:
RFC 5905 describes authenticating an NTP packet by combining the packet data with a 128-bit key and hashing the result with MD5. This memo says MD5 does not provide a secure message authentication code and requires that this use be deprecated.

It recommends AES-CMAC, an authentication method specified in RFC 4493, as the replacement.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier NTP method uses MD5 to check packet authenticity. This memo says that method is too weak and recommends AES-CMAC instead.

sections.title: Using AES-CMAC
sections.content:
If NTP authentication is implemented, AES-CMAC must be computed over every field in the NTP header and any extension fields present in the packet. The key must be an AES-128 key that is 128 bits long, and the resulting tag must be at least 128 bits long.

The hosts share the symmetric key outside the protocol. Its identifier, type, and key value must all match for the hosts to authenticate packets successfully. An older implementation without AES-CMAC will not send or accept packets authenticated with such a key.
sections.plainLanguage: Both hosts need matching key information and AES-CMAC support. The check covers the NTP header and any extension fields, and the packet carries an authentication tag.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo directs readers to the AES-CMAC specification and the cited NIST guidance for details about the method's security guarantees. It makes no IANA changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC directs implementers to the AES-CMAC specification for its security details. It does not change any IANA registry.
